opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
What caught me today was the Gospel of John 12:1–11. When the sister of Lazarus anointed Jesus’ feet with expensive oil, nard, and dried them with her hair. Judas is infuriated, but Jesus tells him to leave her alone—let her keep this for the day of my burial.

For a moment, I wondered—was this the sinful woman who also washed His feet with her tears, wiped them with her hair, and anointed them with perfume? Then I realized they both happened, as well as an additional anointing by an unnamed woman recorded in the Gospel of Matthew and the Gospel of Mark. She pours perfume on His head near Bethany.

So there are three accounts, all slightly different, but pointing to the same inner meaning: repentance, forgiveness, love, devotion, and ultimately preparation for His burial.

We can draw from each of these as models for confession. What actually occurs is what we see in these encounters: coming close to Jesus, kneeling, bringing something costly (our sins), pouring yourself out completely, even using your dignity and identity—like the hair used to dry His feet—and doing so without protecting yourself.

Just bring yourself as you are. Bringing what is real—your costly struggles. Not holding back. Not protecting your image.

You are revealing yourself to Christ, as is.

This is not a time for protection. It is not a time to measure or manage what you give. It is a time to pour it out.

In each of these accounts, Jesus is anointed with oil. Yet at the time of His death, He is buried in haste, and the women plan to return with spices. But when they return, the tomb is empty.

So while we are still alive, why not repent—uncover, release, and draw near to Him. Don’t wait. While we still can, we have the choice to change what may.

Rather than be like the rich man who had everything but ignored the most important aspect of his life—to love. Lazarus lay at his gate, and he never helped him, even though he had the chance. He never saw it.

Only after he died, in torment, did he look up across the great chasm—realizing he could no longer cross from here to there or there to here.

No movement. No undoing.

This is final.
